# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations, but they differ in their approach to data ownership, scalability, and cost. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Slack to Element, particularly those who value data sovereignty and self-hosting capabilities.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full control over their data, while Slack's data ownership policies are more restrictive.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable, but requires more effort to configure, while Slack's scalability is more straightforward.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations available
* Good mobile app support
* Robust customer support
* Limited data ownership and control
### Element
* Self-hosting capabilities
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Highly customizable
* Free and open-source
* Steeper learning curve and more technical expertise required

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams who prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, and are willing to pay a per-user fee. It's particularly suitable for small to medium-sized teams who don't require advanced customization or self-hosting capabilities.
Element is a good choice for teams who value data sovereignty, self-hosting, and customization. It's particularly suitable for larger teams or organizations with advanced technical expertise, who require end-to-end encryption and are willing to invest time in setup and maintenance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack Export Tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's conversations and data.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your team's needs.
3. Use the Element Import Tool to import your Slack data into Element, which supports JSON files.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations required by your team.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires significant technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's user interface can be overwhelming for non-technical users. However, for teams who value data sovereignty and self-hosting, Element is a clear choice, and we recommend switching from Slack to Element if you have the technical expertise and require advanced customization and security features.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't require advanced integrations and want to save on costs.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who value data sovereignty and self-hosting capabilities.
* Large teams (over 50 users) who require end-to-end encryption and advanced customization.
* Teams who don't require phone or video conferencing features.
* Teams who have the technical expertise to set up and maintain an Element server.

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any per-user fees. However, you'll need to cover the costs of hosting and maintaining your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element has a steeper learning curve and requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, it offers more advanced customization and security features.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element has a wide range of integrations available, including GitHub, Trello, and Google Drive. However, its integration ecosystem is not as large as Slack's.
### Does Element offer end-to-end encryption?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations, which means that only the participants in a conversation can read the messages.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack Export Tool and import it into Element using the Element Import Tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are both communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those valuing data ownership and self-hosting capabilities. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over data and costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it a good choice for large teams, while Slack's scalability is more dependent on its proprietary infrastructure.
* Integration Difference: Mattermost has a more extensive API and supports more customization options, including integrations with other tools, whereas Slack has a more limited set of API options.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with other tools
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited customization options
### Mattermost
* Self-hosting option for data control
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Supports large-scale deployments
* Free, open-source option
* Steeper learning curve due to customization options

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require a high degree of customization. It's also a good fit for teams that are already invested in the Slack ecosystem and don't want to migrate to a new platform. Mattermost, on the other hand, is a better choice for larger teams or organizations that require more control over their data and customization options. It's also a good fit for teams that are looking for a self-hosted solution and have the technical expertise to support it.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or using a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, including channels, users, and messages.
4. Configure any necessary integrations or customizations in Mattermost.
5. Test your Mattermost setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data. However, it's worth noting that Mattermost can be more complex to set up and manage, particularly for smaller teams without dedicated technical resources. For teams that value ease of use and don't require a high degree of customization, Slack may still be a better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need extensive customization options
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that require more control over their data
* Large teams (50+ users) that need a self-hosted solution for scalability and cost savings
* Teams that require a high degree of customization and integration with other tools
* Organizations with strict data ownership and compliance requirements

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option, allowing teams to host their own servers and have full control over their data.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free and open-source, with a self-hosted option available at no cost.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers an import tool that allows teams to migrate their Slack data, including channels, users, and messages.
### Does Mattermost have the same features as Slack?
Mattermost offers many of the same features as Slack, including chat, file sharing, and integrations, but may not have all of the same features or integrations.
### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Mattermost can be suitable for small teams, but may require more technical expertise to set up and manage, particularly for self-hosted options.

* Data Ownership: Element allows users to have full control over their data, whereas Discord stores user data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Discord is generally easier to set up, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable due to its decentralized architecture, whereas Discord can become costly for large teams.

# Notion vs AppFlowy

## Overview

Notion is a popular all-in-one workspace combining notes, wikis, databases, and project management. AppFlowy is an open-source alternative with a local-first architecture that keeps your data on your device or own server.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; AppFlowy is completely free
- **Data location**: AppFlowy stores data locally by default; Notion stores on their servers
- **Offline support**: AppFlowy works fully offline; Notion requires internet for most features
- **Privacy**: AppFlowy does not collect usage data; Notion privacy policy allows data analysis
- **Feature parity**: Notion has more polished features and AI tools; AppFlowy is rapidly catching up

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | AppFlowy |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### AppFlowy

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy](https://github.com/AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy) * ~59k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion suits teams wanting a polished workspace with AI writing tools and seamless collaboration without managing infrastructure.

**Choose AppFlowy if:** AppFlowy is ideal for privacy-conscious individuals, users in regions with data sovereignty requirements, or anyone needing offline-first functionality.

## Migration Path

Export your Notion workspace as Markdown plus CSV files, then import the Markdown files into AppFlowy. Database structures will need to be recreated manually.

## Our Take

AppFlowy is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your AppFlowy instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted AppFlowy will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is AppFlowy free to use?
Yes. AppFlowy is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to AppFlowy?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the AppFlowy import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does AppFlowy get regular updates?
Yes. AppFlowy has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use AppFlowy without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if AppFlowy development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [AppFlowy](https://appflowy.io) before making decisions.*

* Scalability: Logseq is designed to be highly scalable and can handle large amounts of data, while Notion can become slower with very large datasets.

* Wide range of features and templates
* Large user community and support
* Integrates well with other tools and services

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
